On May 4, 1970, hundreds of Ohio National Guard troops occupied the Kent State University campus. Armed with M-1 rifles, bayonets, tear gas, and live ammunition, their presence transformed an already tense campus into a powder keg. For many students, the war in Vietnam had suddenly come home. Protests had erupted across the country following President Nixon's expansion of the war into Cambodia, but few could have imagined just how deadly the confrontation at Kent State would become.

item.title: Truth under pressure: Life as an investigative journalist in Kyrgyzstan | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
What does it mean to practice investigative journalism in Kyrgyzstan? What are the consequences of holding politicians accountable for corruption? Here, practicing journalism can be life-threatening.
Instead of being celebrated as heroes, journalists in the Central Asian republic of Kyrgyzstan often face threats. Their private lives suffer, as does their safety—and sometimes even their very lives wind up on the line. Ali Toktakunov, one of Kyrgyzstan’s best-known investigative journalists, stands up to the ruling elite by exposing a corruption case. But when his most important informant is shot dead, Toktakunov flees to the Czech Republic. The tension between his personal life and his work is brought to light by director Samara Sagynbaeva—who is also his wife. Her diary-style documentary paints a portrait of a courageous journalist. At the same time, the film serves as a reminder of the fragility of democracy and the rule of law in a country where freedom of expression is by no means a given.

item.author: Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
In this special live recording from the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, July 2026, the central question discussed was what do mathematicians really value about doing mathematics in the first place?
“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time. For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/
--------- 00:00 – Welcome, Introductions & the AlphaProof/IMO Milestone 04:25 – The Erdős Problems & AI's First Real Proof 09:43 – Is Proof the Point? Math as Storytelling 15:44 – Mathematical Intuition and "Moral Truth" 20:19 – AI Homework and the "Double-Peak" Test Scores 26:22 – Will Math Still Be Fun? Debating the Singularity 29:47 – The Forklift Analogy: Why Struggle Matters 34:44 – Audience Q&A: Access to AI and Open-Source Tools 39:37 – Q&A: Grad School, Tenure, and Whether to Use AI 44:52 – Q&A: Low-Hanging Fruit and the Future of Discovery ---------
Mathematicians are witnessing a profound shift in their field. AI systems are now producing proofs, spotting connections between distant fields, and, in a few cases, solving problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. The pace of progress over the past several months has raised challenging questions: What can AI systems actually do? And what happens to the more human, creative aspects of the field once machines can match – or exceed – people at problem-solving?
In this special live episode of The Joy of Why, recorded at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia on July 26, 2026, hosts Janna Levin and Steven Strogatz are joined by three mathematicians responding to the rise of AI in math: Akshay Venkatesh at the Institute for Advanced Study; Ravi Vakil at Stanford University and president of the American Mathematical Society; and Alex Kontorovich at Rutgers University. Together they discuss what recent AI-generated proofs really demonstrate, what will be gained and lost as mathematics becomes more machine-assisted at the frontier, and what this means for the next generation of mathematicians. The conversation turns to a deeper question: What do mathematicians value about doing mathematics in the first place? The answer involves grappling with what proof and understanding really mean, and with the surprising importance of storytelling.

Quantum Computers are looking set to be the next revolution. For the past few years, investors have been piling their money into AI. Now, they're turning their attention to quantum computers.
Quantum computers have the ability to solve problems exponentially faster than regular computers, taking mathematical problems that would have taken billions of years to solve, and solving them in days or even hours.
The implications of this are frightening - particularly when we think about the security of the financial system. The infrastructure of the global financial system is built to withstand cyber attacks from regular computers. But quantum computers are a different ball-game. Cybersecurity is being turned on its head, and the global finance network is scrambling to update its security to withstand quantum attacks, before its too late.
In this video we'll break down how the financial system - your bank account, stock exchange, apps on your phone, pension funds etc - stay secure. item.title: Laughing to survive - On tour with the Palestine Comedy Club | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Six Palestinian comedians go on tour in Israel and the Palestinian territories. What begins as a stand-up comedy show evolves, in the face of terror and war, into a plea for humanity.
Although there are no comedy clubs -- and hardly any stand-up comedy -- in the Palestinian territories, comedian Alaa Shehada decides to found a stand-up comedy troupe, along with other local artists. Their goal? To develop a program that combines Western comedic traditions with Palestinian narrative forms, to perform in front of an audience.
Despite cultural and security hurdles, the group’s six members—each holding a different travel permit—manage to stage a tour of theaters in the Palestinian territories and in Israel. The shows are well attended, and the group begins to gain attention, even internationally.
Eventually, they receive an invitation to London for a series of performances. These are set to begin on, of all days, October 7, 2023. Against the backdrop of Hamas’ terrorist attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, the comedians face the challenge of performing before an increasingly polarized audience in the UK.
Palestine Comedy Club is a film about the search for humor in everyday life under excruciating conditions—and the attempt to forge connections through shared laughter.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. Mathematicians are witnessing a profound shift in their field. AI systems are now producing proofs, spotting connections between distant fields, and, in a few cases, solving problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. The pace of progress over the past several months has raised challenging questions: What can AI systems actually do? And what happens to the more human, creative aspects of the field once machines can match – or exceed – people at problem-solving?
In this special live episode of The Joy of Why, recorded at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia on July 26, 2026, hosts Janna Levin and Steven Strogatz are joined by three mathematicians responding to the rise of AI in math: Akshay Venkatesh at the Institute for Advanced Study; Ravi Vakil at Stanford University and president of the American Mathematical Society; and Alex Kontorovich at Rutgers University. Together they discuss what recent AI-generated proofs really demonstrate, what will be gained and lost as mathematics becomes more machine-assisted at the frontier, and what this means for the next generation of mathematicians. The conversation turns to a deeper question: What do mathematicians value about doing mathematics in the first place? The answer involves grappling with what proof and understanding really mean, and with the surprising importance of storytelling.

item.title: Black people in Nazi Germany - Lionel Romney's survival in a concentration camp | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Afro-Caribbean sailor Lionel Romney survived eleven months in a concentration camp. His story illustrates how Black people were systematically persecuted under the Nazi regime.
Lionel Romney was born in Santo Domingo in 1912 and raised on Sint Maarten. As a young man, he signed on to a cargo ship to see the world. But his longing for freedom turned into a tragic odyssey. Caught up in the turmoil of World War II, his ship came under fire and sunk. The crew survived. But Lionel was taken prisoner by the Italians. After years in various camps, he was eventually deported to the Mauthausen concentration camp. He survived there for eleven months, before American troops liberated the camp. Decades after the war, Lionel Romney entrusted his memories to his daughter, Mary. Her journey from the Caribbean through Italy to Austria forms the framework of the film, which shines a light on a chapter of European history that has been suppressed to this day: the reality of life for Black people under National Socialism. This reality was marked by colonial continuities, racism, forced labor, and political arbitrariness. Lionel Romney was one of many who were exploited for propaganda purposes or subjected to persecution. Experts such as Clarence Lusane, Katharina Oguntoye, Walter Sauer, and Serge Bilé discuss historical perspectives. Archival footage and artistic reenactments weave together, in a rich visual narrative.

For many people, the most difficult questions after the deadly terror attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, were not about politics, military strategy, or homeland security. They were questions about God, evil and the potential for darkness within religion itself. And for many, those questions didn’t go away.
In “Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero,” FRONTLINE producer Helen Whitney set out to discover how the religious beliefs of Americans were challenged a year after the attacks.
From survivors who were pulled from the wreckage of the Twin Towers to the widow of a New York City firefighter; from priests and rabbis to security guards and an opera singer; from lapsed Catholics and Jews to Buddhists, Muslims, and atheists, this documentary explored and illuminated the myriad of spiritual questions that came out of the terror, pain, and destruction at Ground Zero.

item.title: Daily life in a German prison | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Around 44,000 men and women are incarcerated in Germany's approximately 170 prisons. About 1,800 are serving time for murder, while most are incarcerated for assault, robbery, theft or drug-related offenses.
One of them is Marcel M., serving time in Berlin's Plötzensee Prison. A repeat offender, he calls it "Stealing, stealing, stealing — all for the addiction." Marcel was living with a drug addiction, it's landed him in prison several times. He's already spent a third of his life behind bars. He wants this to be the last time. Marcel is finishing up his training in the prison's car workshop. After he's released, he wants to find a steady job. Plötzensee Prison in Berlin has space for around 650 places for male inmates. Some 250 correctional officers look after the prisoners in shifts. Helena Emisch has worked there for eight years now. She knows the prison inside and out and aims each day to strike a balance between professional distance and connecting with the inmates. Locking and unlocking cells, head counts, distributing packages, administering medication and supervising the yard before recreational time are all part of her job. She also conducts cell searches, looking for drugs and other illegal items. "It's a game of cat and mouse between us and the inmates. Sometimes we win, sometimes they do," she says. Vechta is home to the only women's prison in the German state of Lower Saxony. Melanie F. is one of around 300 inmates there. She, too, turned to crime because of her drug use. She's now serving her third prison sentence — this time for armed robbery. "Prison was hell for me, and prison saved me," she says. Melanie now describes the prison as her substitute family. She feels more at home at Vechta Prison than she does in the outside world. Inside, she's now completed her drug treatment and is currently training to work as a painter.
